items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves a free meal to all visitors

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice, originated by Guru Nanak, institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru) who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him
A meal restricted to initiated Khalsa Sikhs

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level to eat — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — recently in Ukraine, Turkey, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. The simple physical act of sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: Confucianism is not always classed as a religion

options.text: A monotheistic religion with a creator god

An ethical and philosophical tradition centred on social relationships and self-cultivation — often called a religion in Western frameworks but treated as philosophy and ethics in Chinese tradition; rituals (li) and the cultivation of virtues (ren, yi, zhi, xin) are central

items.reveal:
Confucius (Kongzi, 551-479 BCE) taught a system of social ethics based on five key relationships: ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, friend-friend. Filial piety (xiao) anchors the family; ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety) anchor the broader ethical life.

The Analects (Lunyu) is the foundational text, compiled by disciples. Mencius (4th century BCE) and Xunzi (3rd century BCE) developed the tradition. Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi, 12th century) systematised it for later imperial China.

Whether Confucianism is a religion depends on the definition of religion — it includes ritual, sage veneration and cosmological elements but no creator god or afterlife doctrine.
items.why: Western categories ('religion', 'philosophy', 'ethics') don't always fit non-Western traditions. Confucianism's case shows how the very question of what counts as religion is partly a cultural artefact — and changes the answer.

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (Reform Jews observe 7 days worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora (Orthodox/Conservative).

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night outside Israel). The Haggadah ('the telling') is the text recited — recounting the Exodus story through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions.

'Next year in Jerusalem' closes the Seder. The festival's themes of liberation have shaped social movements: the African American spiritual tradition (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but a structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.
